Metabotropic effects are also important for arousal, attention, hunger, thirst, and emotion—functions that arise slowly and last longer than a sensation.","paragraphIndex":20031,"printedPages":[53]},{"label":"Explanation and consequence","explanation":"Because different receptors control different functions, drugs can have specialized effects on behavior.","paragraphIndex":20032,"printedPages":[54]},{"label":"Additional explanation","explanation":"A given receptor can have different effects for different people, or even in different parts of one person’s brain, because of differences in the hundreds of proteins that surround synapses, tether the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron, and guide neurotransmitter molecules to their receptors. Soon investigators found that the brain produces its own neuropeptides, now known as endorphins (a contraction of endo genous m orphines ), that bind to the same receptors as opiates.","paragraphIndex":20033,"printedPages":[54]},{"label":"Further evidence","explanation":"This discovery was important because it indicated that opiates relieve pain by acting on receptors in the brain as well as in the skin.","paragraphIndex":20034,"printedPages":[54]}],"status":"whole_book_source_structured_classroom_notes","basis":"uploaded_textbook_pdf_and_markdown","evidenceMethod":"source_heading_facts","sourceFactCount":9,"editorialVerification":"source-aligned, individual paraphrase review pending","followUpExplanation":"Whereas most ionotropic effects depend on either glutamate or GABA, metabotropic synapses use many chemicals, including dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, neuropeptides... and sometimes glutamate and GABA too.","followUpParagraphIndex":20029,"studyDepth":"detailed_existing","editorialLesson":{"text":"A neurotransmitter's binding to a postsynaptic receptor starts a response in the receiving cell. The same transmitter can have different effects in different tissues, because the receptor subtype and downstream machinery differ.","paragraphIndex":800406,"kind":"individually_written_classroom_explanation","level":"contextual_clarification","sourceHeadingId":"bp14-m2-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70,"editorialStatus":"individual_topic_specific_explanation_drafted_from_source_topic_map","evidenceBasis":"Supplied Kalat 14e PDF and matching Markdown; existing source-extracted paragraphs kept as separate verifiable references","needsIndependentReview":true,"guidedExplanation":{"steps":[{"label":"Rapid responses","explanation":"At an ionotropic receptor, transmitter binding changes an ion channel directly. The resulting ion flow can depolarize or hyperpolarize the membrane on a short timescale. These immediate voltage shifts contribute to the EPSPs and IPSPs the neuron integrates.","paragraphIndex":900425},{"label":"Slower modulation","explanation":"Metabotropic receptors influence intracellular signaling systems, often through G proteins and second messengers. Rather than simply opening one channel, they may change channel sensitivity, protein activity, or how the cell responds to later inputs.","paragraphIndex":900426},{"label":"Why one transmitter has several effects","explanation":"A transmitter is not inherently excitatory or inhibitory everywhere. Its effects depend on receptor subtype, the receiving cell's internal machinery, and the circuit in which the synapse operates. Thus a drug acting on a widely used transmitter may produce several different behavioral effects.","paragraphIndex":900427}],"overview":"Receptor binding is the start of a response, not the whole response. Follow the signal from the released chemical to the changed activity of the receiving cell to understand how the same transmitter can influence different behaviors.","overviewIndex":900424,"sourcePrintedPage":52,"sourcePdfPage":70,"source":"Individual textbook-grounded explanatory walkthrough; essential mechanisms and limitations only"}}},{"headingId":"bp14-m2-2-h08","title":"Inactivation and Reuptake of Neurotransmitters","level":2,"parentId":"bp14-m2-2-h02","printedPage":54,"pdfPage":72,"explanation":"One is recycling, so that the presynaptic neuron has transmitters available for release again.","paragraphIndex":20035,"bullets":[{"label":"Important distinction","explanation":"Although reuptake is efficient, it takes time, and the presynaptic neuron does not reabsorb every molecule it releases.","paragraphIndex":20037,"printedPages":[54]},{"label":"Underlying mechanism","explanation":"The reuptake process varies among individuals and from one brain area to another, but it is slower than reuptake of glutamate or GABA. In many cases the slow reuptake is a benefit, because it enables the chemicals to build up enough concentration to have significant effects on their receptors.","paragraphIndex":20038,"printedPages":[55]},{"label":"Explanation and consequence","explanation":"Because resynthesizing these large molecules takes time, a neuron can temporarily exhaust its supply.","paragraphIndex":20039,"printedPages":[55]},{"label":"Effect or outcome","explanation":"Stimulant drugs, including amphetamine and cocaine, inhibit the transporters for dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine, decreasing reuptake and prolonging the effects of the neurotransmitters.","paragraphIndex":20040,"printedPages":[55]},{"label":"Important implication","explanation":"Most antidepressant drugs also block reuptake of one or more neurotransmitters, but more weakly than amphetamine and cocaine do. Methylphenidate blocks the reuptake of dopamine in the same way that cocaine does, at the same brain receptors.","paragraphIndex":20041,"printedPages":[55]},{"label":"A methadone pill","explanation":"A methadone pill increases arousal at first, but a few hours later the user may experience reduced energy and motivation.","paragraphIndex":20042,"printedPages":[55]}],"status":"whole_book_source_structured_classroom_notes","basis":"uploaded_textbook_pdf_and_markdown","evidenceMethod":"source_heading_facts","sourceFactCount":10,"editorialVerification":"source-aligned, individual paraphrase review pending","followUpExplanation":"The choline diffuses back to the presynaptic neuron, which reattaches it to form acetylcholine again.","followUpParagraphIndex":20036,"studyDepth":"detailed_existing","editorialLesson":{"text":"A chemical message must eventually end. The transmitting system removes or inactivates released transmitter through transporter-mediated reuptake, enzymatic breakdown, diffusion, or uptake by surrounding cells. Ending the message allows a synapse to respond clearly to the next signal. After feeling discouraged all day, he awoke the following night at 3 a.m. with the same idea, rushed to the laboratory, and performed the experiment.","Despite Loewi’s work, most researchers over the next three decades continued to believe that most synapses were electrical and that chemical synapses were the exception.","Finally, in the 1950s, researchers established that chemical transmission predominates throughout the nervous system. A small number of electrical synapses do exist, however, as discussed later in this module.","Understanding the chemical events at a synapse is fundamental to understanding the nervous system.","As we do, we also consider drugs that affect certain steps in this process.","Most members of the animal kingdom have all or nearly all the same transmitters that humans have. Ctenophores (Figure 2.11), possibly representative of the earliest, most primitive animals, apparently have only one neurotransmitter, glutamate.","Glutamate acts even in the plant kingdom, transmitting messages to help the plant react to a damaged part.","The oddest transmitter is nitric oxide (chemical formula NO), a gas released by many small local neurons. (Do not confuse nitric oxide, NO, with nitrous oxide, N 2 O, sometimes known as “laughing gas.”) Nitric oxide is toxic in large quantities and difficult to make in a laboratory.","In addition to influencing other neurons, nitric oxide dilates the nearby blood vessels, thereby increasing blood flow to that brain area. The amino acid tryptophan, the precursor to serotonin, crosses the blood–brain barrier by a special transport system that it shares with other large amino acids.","However, tryptophan competes with more abundant amino acids, including phenylalanine, that share the same transport system, so eating more protein is not a reliable way to add tryptophan to the brain.","One way to increase tryptophan in the brain is to decrease consumption of phenylalanine. It has no therapeutic use, but researchers sometimes use it to study the functions of dopamine.","Chemical synapses usually keep a supply of neurotransmitter ready in the presynaptic terminal. Most transmitters are synthesized near their release site, and many are packed into small membrane-bound vesicles. Storing the molecules close to the synapse lets a neuron release them when the appropriate signal arrives.","Vesicles are tiny, nearly spherical packets in the presynaptic terminal. They hold a high concentration of neurotransmitter molecules until the cell releases their contents into the synaptic cleft.","The textbook also describes a pool of neurotransmitter outside these packets in the terminal. Storage and the chemical supply of a transmitter are therefore related but are not identical processes.","An action potential by itself does not release the neurotransmitter at the end of the axon.","The calcium entry causes exocytosis —a burst of release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic neuron.","The released neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft to the postsynaptic membrane, where it attaches to a receptor.","The neurotransmitter takes no more than 0.01 ms to diffuse across the cleft, which is only 20 to 30 nanometers (nm) wide. For many years, investigators believed that each neuron released just one neurotransmitter, but later researchers found that many, probably most, neurons release a combination of two or more transmitters.","simultaneously release an excitatory transmitter and an inhibitory transmitter, the equivalent of saying “yes” and “no” at the same time.","In contrast to the voltage-gated channels along an axon, the channels controlled by a neurotransmitter are transmitter-gated or ligand-gated. (A ligand is a chemical that binds to something.) When the neurotransmitter attaches, it opens a channel.","Whereas most ionotropic effects depend on either glutamate or GABA, metabotropic synapses use many chemicals, including dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, neuropeptides... and sometimes glutamate and GABA too.","However, a cluster of related axons might fire a burst of action potentials, releasing a cloud of the neuromodulator that diffuses to many receptors.","Metabotropic synapses are suited for more enduring effects such as taste, smell, and pain, where the exact timing is less important. Metabotropic effects are also important for arousal, attention, hunger, thirst, and emotion—functions that arise slowly and last longer than a sensation.","Because different receptors control different functions, drugs can have specialized effects on behavior.","A given receptor can have different effects for different people, or even in different parts of one person’s brain, because of differences in the hundreds of proteins that surround synapses, tether the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron, and guide neurotransmitter molecules to their receptors. Soon investigators found that the brain produces its own neuropeptides, now known as endorphins (a contraction of endo genous m orphines ), that bind to the same receptors as opiates.","This discovery was important because it indicated that opiates relieve pain by acting on receptors in the brain as well as in the skin.","One is recycling, so that the presynaptic neuron has transmitters available for release again.","The choline diffuses back to the presynaptic neuron, which reattaches it to form acetylcholine again.","Although reuptake is efficient, it takes time, and the presynaptic neuron does not reabsorb every molecule it releases.","The reuptake process varies among individuals and from one brain area to another, but it is slower than reuptake of glutamate or GABA. In many cases the slow reuptake is a benefit, because it enables the chemicals to build up enough concentration to have significant effects on their receptors.","Because resynthesizing these large molecules takes time, a neuron can temporarily exhaust its supply.","Stimulant drugs, including amphetamine and cocaine, inhibit the transporters for dopamine, serotonin, and norepinephrine, decreasing reuptake and prolonging the effects of the neurotransmitters.","Most antidepressant drugs also block reuptake of one or more neurotransmitters, but more weakly than amphetamine and cocaine do. Methylphenidate blocks the reuptake of dopamine in the same way that cocaine does, at the same brain receptors.","A methadone pill increases arousal at first, but a few hours later the user may experience reduced energy and motivation.","Don’t send it again.” A couple of mechanisms in the nervous system serve that function.","First, many presynaptic terminals have receptors sensitive to the same transmitter they release.","These receptors are known as autoreceptors —receptors that respond to the released transmitter by inhibiting further synthesis and release. of the Vertebrate Nervous System","kind":"detailed_source_grounded_notes","printedStart":66,"printedEnd":80,"pdfStart":84,"pdfEnd":98,"content":[{"type":"paragraph","text":"The nervous system can be described by directional terms and by its major divisions. The spinal cord, autonomic nervous system, hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain participate in different but interconnected functions."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Build a mental map of the major structures rather than memorizing names without context. Pay particular attention to how the thalamus, hypothalamus, basal ganglia, hippocampus, and ventricles fit into the larger organization."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m3-1-study-1","text":"The basic map"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The central nervous system includes the brain and spinal cord; the peripheral nervous system includes structures outside them. Sensory routes carry information toward central processing, while motor routes influence muscles and organs. Anatomical words such as anterior, posterior, dorsal, ventral, medial, and lateral specify location relative to the body or nervous system. Learn these directions before memorizing structures: an accurate map helps prevent mixing up nearby names that have very different functions."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m3-1-study-2","text":"Spinal cord, autonomic system, and brainstem"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The spinal cord carries signals between body and brain and participates in reflexes. The autonomic nervous system regulates functions such as heart activity, digestion, and glandular secretion. Its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions often support different bodily demands but are not simply permanent 'on' and 'off' systems. In the hindbrain, structures including the medulla, pons, and cerebellum support vital regulation and coordinated activity. The midbrain participates in sensory processing and movement-related functions."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m3-1-study-3","text":"Forebrain structures worth distinguishing"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The thalamus is a major relay and processing hub for many sensory pathways. The hypothalamus helps regulate basic bodily needs and works closely with the pituitary gland. Basal ganglia contribute to selection and control of actions; the basal forebrain has broad influences on cortical function. The hippocampus is especially important to memory, while the cerebral cortex supports many aspects of perception, cognition, and action. The ventricles are fluid-filled cavities connected to the circulation of cerebrospinal fluid. These descriptions are functional signposts, not one-function-per-structure definitions."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m3-1-study-4","text":"How to study anatomy effectively"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Study pathways instead of memorizing only lists. For example, ask where a sensory signal enters the spinal cord, which central structures process it, and how an action command reaches a muscle. For any structure, identify where it sits, major connections, and the kind of evidence linking it to a function. Anatomical labels become meaningful when they explain why injury at different locations has different effects."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h01","text":"Terminology to Describe the Nervous System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For vertebrates, we distinguish the central nervous system from the peripheral nervous system (Figure 3.1).","sourcePrintedPage":66,"sourcePdfPage":84,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"peripheral nervous system (PNS) connects the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body.","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Part of the PNS is the somatic nervous system , which consists of the axons conveying messages from the sense organs to the CNS and from the CNS to the muscles.","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Another part of the PNS, the autonomic nervous system , controls the body’s organs.","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A special part of the autonomic nervous system is the enteric nervous system , which controls the digestive system .","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the nervous system is threedimensional, we need more terms to describe it.","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, when humans evolved upright posture, the position of the head changed relative to the spinal cord.","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Consequently, the dorsal–ventral axis of the human brain is at a right angle to the dorsal–ventral axis of the spinal cord.","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h02","text":"The Spinal Cord"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The spinal cord communicates with all the sense organs and muscles except those of the head.","sourcePrintedPage":68,"sourcePdfPage":86,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cell bodies of the sensory neurons are in clusters of neurons outside the spinal cord, called the dorsal root ganglia . ( Ganglia is the plural of ganglion , a cluster of neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":68,"sourcePdfPage":86,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In most cases, a neuron cluster outside the CNS is called a ganglion, and a cluster inside the CNS is called a nucleus.) Cell bodies of the motor neurons are inside the spinal cord.","sourcePrintedPage":68,"sourcePdfPage":86,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many neurons from the gray matter of the spinal cord send axons to the brain or to other parts of the spinal cord through the white matter , containing myelinated axons.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each segment of the spinal cord sends sensory information to the brain and receives motor commands from the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If the spinal cord is cut at a given segment, the brain loses sensation from that segment and below.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h03","text":"The Autonomic Nervous System"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The autonomic nervous system consists of neurons that receive information from and send commands to the heart, intestines, and other organs.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the sympathetic ganglia are closely linked, they often act as a single system “in sympathy” with one another, although certain events activate some parts more than others.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The parasympathetic nervous system , sometimes called the “rest and digest” system, facilitates vegetative, nonemergency responses.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate, and the parasympathetic nervous system decreases it.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The parasympathetic nervous system increases digestive activity, whereas the sympathetic nervous system decreases it.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike the ganglia in the sympathetic system, the parasympathetic ganglia are not arranged in a chain near the spinal cord.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parasympathetic activity decreases heart rate, increases digestive rate, and, in general, conserves energy.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most sympathetic nervous system axons release norepinephrine, although a few, such as those onto the sweat glands, use acetylcholine.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the two systems use different transmitters, certain drugs excite or inhibit one system or the other.","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the flow of sinus fluids is a parasympathetic response, drugs that block the parasympathetic system inhibit sinus flow.","sourcePrintedPage":70,"sourcePdfPage":88,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Certain decongestant pills containing pseudoephedrine have been withdrawn or restricted because of their potential for abuse.","sourcePrintedPage":70,"sourcePdfPage":88,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h04","text":"The Hindbrain"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some neuroscientists prefer terms with Greek roots: rhombencephalon (hindbrain), mesencephalon (midbrain), and prosencephalon (forebrain).","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The hindbrain , the posterior part of the brain, consists of the medulla, the pons, and the cerebellum.","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The medulla and pons, the midbrain, and certain central structures of the forebrain constitute the brainstem (Figure 3.8).","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In elephants, the trigeminal nerve that receives sensations from the face is huge because it innervates the trunk, a highly sensitive structure for elephants .","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because opiate receptors, which suppress activity, are abundant in the medulla, opiates can produce a dangerous decrease in breathing and heart rate.","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum is a large hindbrain structure with many deep folds.","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is one of the first brain areas to start developing and one of the last to complete development .","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum has long been known for its contributions to the control of movement, and many older textbooks describe the cerebellum as important for “balance and coordination.” True, people with cerebellar damage are clumsy and lose their balance, but the functions of the cerebellum extend far beyond balance and coordination.","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One hypothesis is that the cerebellum’s primary function is to detect sequences of events .","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h05","text":"The Midbrain"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"As the name implies, the midbrain is between the hindbrain and the forebrain, although in adult mammals the forebrain surrounds it.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The roof of the midbrain is called the tectum . ( Tectum is the Latin word for “roof.” The same root occurs in the geological term plate tectonics .) The swellings on each side of the tectum are the superior colliculus and the inferior colliculus (Figures 3.8 and 3.10).","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Under the tectum lies the tegmentum , the intermediate level of the midbrain. (In Latin, tegmentum means a “covering,” such as a rug on the floor.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"midbrain structures.) Another midbrain structure, the substantia nigra , gives rise to a dopamine-containing pathway that facilitates readiness for movement.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h06","text":"The Forebrain"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The forebrain , the most prominent brain area for mammals and birds, consists of two cerebral hemispheres, left and right (Figure 3.11).","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each hemisphere is organized to receive sensory information, mostly from the contralateral (opposite) side of the body.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It controls muscles, mostly on the contralateral side, by way of axons to the spinal cord and the cranial nerve nuclei.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The thalamus is the main source of input to the cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The hypothalamus is essential for control of eating, drinking, temperature control, and reproductive behaviors.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The amygdala is part of a circuit that is central for evaluating emotional information, especially with regard to fear.","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h07","text":"Thalamus"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The thalamus is a pair of structures (left and right) in the center of the forebrain.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Most sensory information goes first to the thalamus, which processes it and sends output to the cerebral cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An exception to this rule is olfactory information, which goes from the olfactory receptors to the olfactory bulbs and then directly to the cerebral cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many nuclei of the thalamus receive their input from a sensory system, such as vision, process it in various ways, and transmit information to an area of the cerebral cortex, as in Figure 3.14.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Another function of the thalamus relates to memory.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When you hold information in working memory, activity bounces back and forth between the frontal cortex and the thalamus .","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h08","text":"Hypothalamus and Pituitary Gland"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The hypothalamus , a small area just ventral to the thalamus (Figures 3.10 and 3.12), has widespread connections with the rest of the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Damage in the hypothalamus leads to abnormalities in motivated behaviors, such as feeding, drinking, temperature regulation, sexual behavior, or fighting.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because of these important behavioral effects, the small hypothalamus attracts much research attention.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Partly through nerves and partly by releasing hormones, the hypothalamus conveys messages to the pituitary gland , altering its release of hormones (Figure 3.10).","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h09","text":"Basal Ganglia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The basal ganglia , a group of subcortical structures lateral to the thalamus, include the caudate nucleus, the putamen,","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many authorities include other structures as well, especially the nucleus accumbens.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It has long been known that damage to the basal ganglia impairs movement, as in conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and Huntington’s disease.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The basal ganglia integrate motivational and emotional behavior to increase the vigor of selected actions.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, the role of the basal ganglia extends beyond movement.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They are critical for gradual learning of skills and habits.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h10","text":"Basal Forebrain"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A structure on the ventral surface of the forebrain, the nucleus basalis , receives input from the hypothalamus and basal ganglia and sends axons that release acetylcholine to widespread areas in the cerebral cortex (Figure 3.16).","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The nucleus basalis is a key system for arousal, wakefulness, and attention.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Patients with Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s disease have impairments of attention and intellect because of inactivity or deterioration in the nucleus basalis.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h11","text":"Hippocampus"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We consider the hippocampus in more detail in the chapter on memory.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The gist of that discussion is that the hippocampus is critical for memories, especially memories for individual events.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is also essential for monitoring where you are and where you are going.","sourcePrintedPage":75,"sourcePdfPage":93,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h12","text":"The Ventricles"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The canal persists into adulthood as the central canal in the center of the spinal cord, and as the ventricles , four fluid-filled cavities within the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":77,"sourcePdfPage":95,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cells called the choroid plexus along the walls of the four ventricles produce cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) , a clear fluid similar to blood plasma.","sourcePrintedPage":77,"sourcePdfPage":95,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"CSF flows from the lateral ventricles to the third and fourth ventricles, and then into the central canal of the spinal cord and the narrow spaces between the brain and the meninges , membranes that surround the brain and spinal cord.","sourcePrintedPage":77,"sourcePdfPage":95,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although the brain has no pain receptors, the meninges do, and meningitis—inflammation of the meninges— is painful.","sourcePrintedPage":77,"sourcePdfPage":95,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It also provides a reservoir of hormones and nutrition for the brain and spinal cord.","sourcePrintedPage":77,"sourcePdfPage":95,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If the flow of CSF is obstructed, it accumulates in the ventricles or in the space between brain and meninges, increasing pressure on the brain.","sourcePrintedPage":77,"sourcePdfPage":95,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m3-1-h13","text":"In Closing: Learning Neuroanatomy"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It will help if you return to review this module as you encounter structures again in later chapters.","sourcePrintedPage":78,"sourcePdfPage":96,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Terms are defined in the module on the page number indicated.","sourcePrintedPage":79,"sourcePdfPage":97,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"They’re also presented in alphabetical order with definitions in the book’s Subject Index/Glossary, at the end of this book.","sourcePrintedPage":79,"sourcePdfPage":97,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Explain why, with reference to the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.","sourcePrintedPage":79,"sourcePdfPage":97,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and the spinal cord.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":66,"sourcePdfPage":84},{"type":"bullet","text":"To follow a map, you must understand north, south, east, and west.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85},{"type":"bullet","text":"As Figure 3.2 and Table 3.1 indicate, dorsal means toward the back and ventral means toward the stomach.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85},{"type":"bullet","text":"The same would be true for you if you crawled on your hands and knees.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 3.2 also illustrates the three ways of taking a plane through the brain, known as horizontal, sagittal, and coronal (or frontal).","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":67,"sourcePdfPage":85},{"type":"bullet","text":"The spinal cord is the part of the CNS within the spinal column.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":68,"sourcePdfPage":86},{"type":"bullet","text":"It is a segmented structure, and each segment has on both its left and right sides a cord depicted in Figures 3.3 and 3.4, the H-shaped gray matter in the center of the cord is densely packed with cell bodies and dendrites.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87},{"type":"bullet","text":"All that information passes through tracts of axons in the spinal cord.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87},{"type":"bullet","text":"The sympathetic nervous system, a network of nerves that prepare the organs for a burst of vigorous activity, consists of chains of ganglia just to the left and right of the spinal cord’s central regions (the thoracic and lumbar areas).","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87},{"type":"bullet","text":"The parasympathetic nervous system is also known as the craniosacral system because it consists of the cranial nerves and nerves from the sacral spinal cord.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":69,"sourcePdfPage":87},{"type":"bullet","text":"The side effects of cold remedies stem from their pro-sympathetic, anti-parasympathetic activities: They increase heart rate, blood pressure, and arousal.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":70,"sourcePdfPage":88},{"type":"bullet","text":"The brain has three major divisions: hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89},{"type":"bullet","text":"The medulla, or medulla oblongata, can be regarded as an enlarged extension of the spinal cord.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89},{"type":"bullet","text":"The cranial nerves originating in the medulla control vital reflexes such as breathing, heart rate, vomiting, salivation, coughing, and sneezing.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with damage to the cerebellum have difficulty with timing, such as judging whether one rhythm is faster than another rhythm.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":71,"sourcePdfPage":89},{"type":"bullet","text":"The midbrain is more prominent in reptiles, amphibians, and fish.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91},{"type":"bullet","text":"Both are important for sensory processing—the inferior colliculus for hearing and the superior colliculus for vision.","headingId":"bp14-m3-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":73,"sourcePdfPage":91},{"type":"bullet","text":"( Cerebrum is a Latin word for Anatomical words such as anterior, posterior, dorsal, ventral, medial, and lateral specify location relative to the body or nervous system. Learn these directions before memorizing structures: an accurate map helps prevent mixing up nearby names that have very different functions.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":66,"sourcePrintedEnd":80,"sourcePdfStart":84,"sourcePdfEnd":98},{"id":"bp14-m3-1-study-2","title":"Spinal cord, autonomic system, and brainstem","text":"The spinal cord carries signals between body and brain and participates in reflexes. The autonomic nervous system regulates functions such as heart activity, digestion, and glandular secretion. Its sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions often support different bodily demands but are not simply permanent 'on' and 'off' systems. In the hindbrain, structures including the medulla, pons, and cerebellum support vital regulation and coordinated activity. The hypothalamus helps regulate basic bodily needs and works closely with the pituitary gland. Basal ganglia contribute to selection and control of actions; the basal forebrain has broad influences on cortical function. The hippocampus is especially important to memory, while the cerebral cortex supports many aspects of perception, cognition, and action. The ventricles are fluid-filled cavities connected to the circulation of cerebrospinal fluid. These descriptions are functional signposts, not one-function-per-structure definitions.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":66,"sourcePrintedEnd":80,"sourcePdfStart":84,"sourcePdfEnd":98},{"id":"bp14-m3-1-study-4","title":"How to study anatomy effectively","text":"Study pathways instead of memorizing only lists. autonomic nervous system consists of neurons that receive information from and send commands to the heart, intestines, and other organs.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":27},{"text":"Because the sympathetic ganglia are closely linked, they often act as a single system “in sympathy” with one another, although certain events activate some parts more than others.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":28},{"text":"The parasympathetic nervous system , sometimes called the “rest and digest” system, facilitates vegetative, nonemergency responses.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":29},{"text":"For example, the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate, and the parasympathetic nervous system decreases it.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":30},{"text":"The parasympathetic nervous system increases digestive activity, whereas the sympathetic nervous system decreases it.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":31},{"text":"Unlike the ganglia in the sympathetic system, the parasympathetic ganglia are not arranged in a chain near the spinal cord.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":32},{"text":"Parasympathetic activity decreases heart rate, increases digestive rate, and, in general, conserves energy.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":33},{"text":"Most sympathetic nervous system axons release norepinephrine, although a few, such as those onto the sweat glands, use acetylcholine.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":34},{"text":"Because the two systems use different transmitters, certain drugs excite or inhibit one system or the other.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":35},{"text":"Because the flow of sinus fluids is a parasympathetic response, drugs that block the parasympathetic system inhibit sinus flow.","printedPage":70,"pdfPage":88,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":36},{"text":"Certain decongestant pills containing pseudoephedrine have been withdrawn or restricted because of their potential for abuse.","printedPage":70,"pdfPage":88,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":37}],"sourceWordCount":498},{"id":"bp14-m3-1-h04","title":"The .","printedPage":71,"pdfPage":89,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":42},{"text":"Because opiate receptors, which suppress activity, are abundant in the the heart, intestines, and other organs.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":27},{"text":"Because the sympathetic ganglia are closely linked, they often act as a single system “in sympathy” with one another, although certain events activate some parts more than others.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":28},{"text":"The parasympathetic nervous system , sometimes called the “rest and digest” system, facilitates vegetative, nonemergency responses.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":29},{"text":"For example, the sympathetic nervous system increases heart rate, and the parasympathetic nervous system decreases it.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":30},{"text":"The parasympathetic nervous system increases digestive activity, whereas the sympathetic nervous system decreases it.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":31},{"text":"Unlike the ganglia in the sympathetic system, the parasympathetic ganglia are not arranged in a chain near the spinal cord.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":32},{"text":"Parasympathetic activity decreases heart rate, increases digestive rate, and, in general, conserves energy.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":33},{"text":"Most sympathetic nervous system axons release norepinephrine, although a few, such as those onto the sweat glands, use acetylcholine.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":34},{"text":"Because the two systems use different transmitters, certain drugs excite or inhibit one system or the other.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":35},{"text":"Because the flow of sinus fluids is a parasympathetic response, drugs that block the parasympathetic system inhibit sinus flow.","printedPage":70,"pdfPage":88,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":36},{"text":"Certain decongestant pills containing pseudoephedrine have been withdrawn or restricted because of their potential for abuse.","printedPage":70,"pdfPage":88,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"selected_textbook_sentence","paragraphIndex":37},{"text":"The sympathetic nervous system, a network of nerves that prepare the organs for a burst of vigorous activity, consists of chains of ganglia just to the left and right of the spinal cord’s central regions cord.","printedPage":69,"pdfPage":87,"source":"user_uploaded_pdf","method":"additional_source_condensed_note","paragraphIndex":109},{"text":"The side effects of cold remedies stem from their
